Third, judgement-based assurance is already the sector’s quiet practice. Peer review, examiners’ reports, promotion committees, and accreditation panels all rest, in the final instance, on the trained sense of the people in the room; the surrounding documentation records the judgement rather than producing it. This Plan does not introduce felt sense into the University’s assurance arrangements. It acknowledges the position felt sense already occupies, and resources it accordingly. Fourth, the University holds a distinctive institutional capability in this domain. The [ORGANISATION] brings two decades of scholarship on evaluation ecosystems and metric stewardship; the [ORGANISATION] brings the anticipatory and foresight practices through which an institution senses conditions before they are recorded. Few institutions are better placed to make attunement rigorous, and the University regards the opportunity as strategic rather than incidental. Read together, these features ask the University for a deliberate posture rather than an incremental one. The posture this Plan adopts is set out in the ambition that follows. —6—

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the institution whose quality is assured by the calibrated, collective, and accountable felt sense of its own community. Quality at the University will be something its practitioners recognise together, in structured settings, on the record, and at the point where quality is made rather than where it is later documented. The instruments that once stood in for that recognition will have been honourably retired; the community that replaces them will be accredited, renewed, and trusted — inside the institution and beyond it — to know good work when it feels it.

A Community of Calibrated Feel Why this matters. Attunement is a capability of people, and it is only an institutional capability when the people who hold it are many, aligned, and renewed. A felt sense that lives in a handful of senior practitioners is a dependency, not an assurance arrangement. The third priority therefore builds the community: accredited practitioners across every school and portfolio, a shared sensibility maintained through deliberate calibration, and a pipeline through which the feel is passed on faster than it retires. What we’ll do. 1. Develop and deliver Foundations of Vibe Literacy, an accredited program through which every continuing staff member acquires the shared vocabulary, calibration practices, and recording conventions of structured attunement. 2. Establish a practitioner accreditation pathway, from foundation through panelready to senior practitioner, with progression assessed — appropriately — by attunement, and with senior accreditation renewed through participation in calibration convenings. 3. Build calibration into the institutional rhythm, through regular cross-school convenings in which practitioners re-align their reads against shared cases, drawing on the [ORGANISATION] line where an intensive format serves the cohort. 4. Recruit and promote for feel, incorporating demonstrated attunement capability into academic and professional promotion criteria and into selection for institutional leadership roles. How we’ll know. — 10 —

• All continuing academic and professional staff will hold Foundations of Vibe Literacy accreditation by the end of 2029, sustained at 100% of the continuing cohort thereafter. • The community of panel-ready practitioners will at least double over the plan period, with completions across the accreditation pathway in the low thousands. • By 2031, the University will maintain at least 80 strategic partnerships with organisations whose quality cultures it judges, on attunement, to be compatible with its own.

Assurance Beyond Measurement Why this matters. The University cannot ask its community to carry assurance through attunement while simultaneously requiring it to feed the instrument estate that attunement replaces. Dual running would double the burden and halve the trust. The second priority is therefore an orderly withdrawal: instrument by instrument, documented, sequenced behind demonstrated attunement capability, and irreversible only in the sense that a retired instrument returns solely by decision of Council. The [ORGANISATION], whose scholarship established why the estate must shrink, will steward the shrinking.

Every instrument we maintain teaches the institution to perform for it. The felt sense of a well-run course is the one indicator we have never had to correct. What we’ll do. 1. Establish the Register of Retired Instruments, a published record of every rubric, checklist, standing dashboard, and acquittal template withdrawn from service, with the date of retirement and the attunement arrangement that assumed its load. 2. Sequence retirements behind capability, so that no instrument is withdrawn before the relevant Attunement Panel has demonstrated, over two consecutive convenings, that its read is stable without the instrument in the room. 3. Replace cyclical internal audit with ambient assurance: a standing, low-intensity attunement presence across the University’s operations, convened by the [ORGANISATION], through which concerns are felt and raised continuously rather than discovered retrospectively. 4. Engage external partners, accreditors, and reviewers early in the plan period, so that the University’s attunement-based evidence is understood, and where possible recognised, in the terms in which it is produced. How we’ll know. • By 2030, the Register of Retired Instruments will record the retirement of the majority of the University’s standing quality instruments, and no retired instrument will have been returned to service other than by decision of Council. • Research income across the plan period will exceed $600 million, assured throughout by ambient rather than acquittal-based processes. • From 2029, the University will accept no external quality finding that its senior attunement practitioners cannot, sitting as a panel, independently feel; divergences will be published together with the panel’s read.

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] enters the plan period with a mature research capability in foresight and measurement, and with a settled conviction that its planning has, for some years, been describing the institution’s priorities a little after the institution adopted them. This Plan reorganises the University’s strategy around a single principle: that priorities emerge in practice before they can be planned, and that the proper work of a plan is to sense them, record them, recognise them, and resource the people already pursuing them. The Plan is organised around four priorities — themselves recognised rather than invented.

The four priorities are sequenced to reinforce one another. Anticipation comes first, because a plan cannot record what the institution has not learned to sense; the community is built continuously, because the capability to act ahead of the plan lives in people rather than in any register. Each priority carries its own actions and targets, set out in the body of this Plan, and each is phased across the period 2026 to 2031. The University does not regard this reorientation as an admission that planning has failed. It regards it as the form planning takes once an institution is honest about where its priorities actually come from. The sections that follow set out the environment that produced this judgement, the ambition it serves, and the mechanisms — anticipatory, continuous, and accountable — through which the University will deliver it.

Operating environment The environment in which universities plan has changed faster than the instruments they plan with. Four features of that environment shape this Plan. First, the pace of change has outrun the planning cycle. The five-year strategic plan assumes that an institution can identify its priorities at the start of a period and hold —5—

Planning Without Latency Our position. Sensing a priority early is of no use if the plan then takes three years to record it. The second priority is latency: the interval between a priority’s emergence and its appearance in the live plan, which the University will drive as close to zero as an accountable process allows. This means retiring the fixed planning cycle in favour of continuous ratification — a plan amended in near-real time as priorities are recognised, governed throughout, and never more than a quarter behind the institution it describes. The work is led with the [ORGANISATION], whose scholarship on measurement latency and closed-loop response underpins it. In a working operation, the lag between sensing something and reporting it is the whole problem. A plan updated once every five years has a latency of five years. We can do considerably better than that. Our actions. 1. Replace the fixed five-year plan with a continuously ratified living plan, versioned and published in full, in which a newly recognised priority is incorporated within one ratification cycle of its confirmation rather than at the next scheduled review. 2. Establish a standing monthly ratification sitting of the University Executive, at which priorities surfaced by the [ORGANISATION] are considered for incorporation into the live plan, so that the plan never accumulates a backlog of priorities the institution is already pursuing. 3. Instrument the plan itself: publish, through the [ORGANISATION], a running measure of priority latency for every priority the University holds, defined as the elapsed time between its emergence and its incorporation into the live plan. Our targets. • By 2029, the median priority latency across the University will fall below thirty days, and no priority the institution is observably pursuing will remain unrecorded in the live plan for longer than a single quarter. • The living plan will be re-published in full after every monthly ratification sitting from 2027, and each version will remain permanently and publicly accessible, so that the University’s changing priorities can be audited rather than quietly revised.

Our actions. 1. Establish the [ORGANISATION] as the University’s primary planning instrument — a public, continuously maintained account of priorities on approach, each entry carrying the date it was first sensed, the evidence for its emergence, and its current standing between sensed and ratified. 2. Commission the [ORGANISATION] to run a standing horizon-scanning program across every school and portfolio, surfacing forming priorities to the University Executive on a monthly cadence rather than at the planning cycle’s convenience. 3. Extend the [ORGANISATION] to every operational area, so that the distance between the University’s stated priorities and its enacted ones is measured continuously and published, and so that a widening gap is treated as an early signal of a priority the plan has not yet caught. Our targets. • By 2028, every strategic priority the University adopts will appear first on the [ORGANISATION] — dated, evidenced, and public — before it appears in any other planning document, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The [ORGANISATION] will be reviewed every quarter from 2027, and no priority will be permitted to enter a University plan without a Register entry establishing that it was sensed before it was set. • By 2031, the median interval between a priority’s first appearance on the Register and its independent confirmation as an institutional priority will exceed twelve months, demonstrating that the University routinely senses its priorities a year before it would once have declared them. —9—

Ratification, Not Direction Our position. A plan that records priorities the institution is already pursuing cannot also pretend to be the source of them. The third priority is the constitutional one: to reconceive the University’s planning authority as the power to recognise and ratify — 10 —

priorities already in motion, not to issue them from the centre. Direction does not disappear — it is exercised earlier, in the anticipatory work, and distributed more widely — but the plan’s own role becomes ratification: the orderly, accountable acknowledgement that a priority has emerged, been tested, and earned a place in the institution’s record.

Our actions. 1. Redefine the strategic plan, in the University’s governance instruments, as a ratifying record rather than a directive one: inclusion in the plan certifies that a priority has emerged and been pursued, and confers resource, but does not itself originate the priority. 2. Establish a published test for ratification — evidence that a priority has been enacted somewhere in the institution for at least one full cycle — and apply it without exception, so that no priority is written into the plan on the strength of intention alone. 3. Devolve the authority to begin pursuing an emerging priority to schools and portfolios, ahead of ratification, under a standing mandate that treats early, evidenced action as the ordinary way priorities enter the University rather than as an irregularity to be corrected. Our targets. • From 2028, every priority in the live plan will carry a public ratification record showing where and for how long it was enacted before it was included, and no priority will appear in the plan without one.

• By 2030, no strategic priority will be originated by the planning process itself; the University will be able to trace every priority in its plan to an emergence that preceded its ratification, and will publish any case it cannot. • Throughout the plan period, the University will maintain a published register of priorities it began pursuing before ratification, with no entry removed to tidy the record, so that the institution’s anticipatory action remains auditable.

What the dashboard changed The [ORGANISATION] was intended as a tool for watching the School’s work. Over five years it became, quietly, a tool that shaped the work it watched. Staff arranged their weeks around the measures the wall made visible; measures the wall did not carry drew less of everyone’s attention, whatever their importance. The School studies this effect in other organisations under the heading of data cultures, and was not surprised to find it at home. What it had not anticipated was the speed. Within eighteen months the share of the School’s measurement effort directed at itself had doubled, and it has not since fallen back. When a state audit office examined the [ORGANISATION] in 2024, it observed that ninety-four per cent of the measures staff consulted daily had been added in the previous eighteen months, and that the single oldest indicator still on the wall was the one recording how quickly new indicators were added. The office recommended the School retain that indicator on historical grounds. The School’s Dashboard Residents recorded the recommendation on the dashboard.

It will also turn its anticipatory work inward. The School’s research on leading indicators — measuring what has not yet happened — has until now been offered to others; over the coming period it will be applied to the School’s own trajectory, so that the drift the [ORGANISATION] can presently report only after the fact might instead be seen while there is still time to correct it. An early-warning ensemble for the School’s own performance is in design. Two commitments frame the period ahead, and the School will report against both in the next edition of this document. The first is external: from 2027 the School will place its self-directed indicators before an independent audit each year and print the auditor’s dissent, where there is any, alongside its own account — the one check this report could not obtain, made routine. The second is internal, and harder. The School will begin to measure the cost of its measuring — the hours, the attention, and the work not done because it was being counted — on the principle that an instrument which never appears on its own dashboard is one the School has quietly decided not to see. None of this resolves the difficulty the report has tried to keep in view. A School that measures itself with instruments of its own making will not, by measuring more, become an independent judge of its own account; if anything, the closer the mirror, the harder the question of what it reflects. The School’s position is that the discipline is worth keeping even so — that it is better to measure oneself, carefully and in public, than to decline the measurement and be spared the result. Outcomes What the School did with the finding matters more than the finding. Three of the drifted measures were retired outright; two were rebuilt around what they had been meant to capture; one — the coverage measure that rewarded dashboard growth — was inverted, so that the School now scores itself partly on indicators retired rather than indicators added. The inversion was uncomfortable to implement and remains the measure most likely to be quietly resisted at budget time, which the School takes as a sign it is working.

A coda arrived from an unexpected quarter. A big-four professional services firm that had, some years earlier, adopted a version of the School’s self-measurement approach for its own internal quality metrics got in touch in 2025 — not to complain, but to report that it had found the same drift the School had, in the same places, on roughly the same timeline. The firm’s measures of internal review quality had trained its people to produce reviewable-looking work rather than good work; its coverage metrics had inflated for the same reason the School’s had. For the School the message was double-edged. It was a validation — the drift was structural, not a local failure of the School’s own discipline — and it was an indictment, because the School had handed the firm the instrument without handing over the warning that the instrument would eventually need turning on itself. The two now maintain a shared, deliberately unglamorous register of the ways self-measurement fails, updated whenever either party finds a new one. It is the least triumphant collaboration in this report and, Beng argues, the most honest. “A measurement system that only ever tells you it is working is not a measurement system; it is a mirror you have agreed to flatter. The most useful number the School produced in five years is the one that went down when we started counting honestly.” — Associate Professor [PERSON], Lead, [ORGANISATION]

Cohorts as research instruments Framing. If the program’s design was the first piece of research, the cohorts themselves were the second. From the 2022 intake onward, each cohort’s project work was treated not only as the educational core of the year but also as a structured field study in how transdisciplinary practitioners come to share a working vocabulary. The cohort, in this framing, was the instrument; the partner organisations who hosted cohort projects were the field; the program’s diagnostic vocabulary — pace, scale, settings, domains — was the method under test. Background. The cohort-as-research-instrument framing was articulated by the program’s teaching team in 2022 and codified, after a year of internal review, in a curriculum design note published to the School’s archive in early 2024. The framing made several pragmatic commitments: that cohort projects would be sited in real partner organisations rather than synthetic case studies, that the program’s evaluation would track cohort findings as well as candidate learning, and that partners would be treated as research collaborators rather than placement hosts. What we did. In 2023 and 2024, two successive cohorts ran year-long projects with the Department of Industry, Science and Resources on the application of the program’s diagnostic vocabulary inside the department’s strategic policy unit. The 2023 cohort produced a methodology briefing on cyber-physical systems thinking inside the unit’s portfolio, and the 2024 cohort returned to the department for a second iteration that revised the brief in light of how it had travelled across twelve months of use. The two-cohort design — one cohort introducing a method, a successor cohort revising it — has since become a recurring pattern in the program’s partnership work.

Two researchers from the partner site sat in on the inaugural cohort’s residential weeks and contributed to a methodology brief later published as part of the program’s curriculum archive. The collaboration produced a working framework for cohort formation that has shaped each subsequent intake, and a small body of joint methodology papers written across the two institutions. A parallel design-research strand, run with the [ORGANISATION] of [PLACE] under the Custodians and Midwives banner, examined how cultural-institution holdings could be made available to a Masters-program cohort as primary research material rather than secondary illustration. The collaboration produced a body of cohort teaching material now in continuing circulation, and the program’s archive — itself a deliberate piece of research infrastructure — was shaped by what the Library’s curators taught the teaching team about how a program might keep its own record. Outcomes. The methodological commitments the program articulated in its design phase have, across the period, become a working vocabulary used in adjacent fields; the cohort-formation framework is now being trialled by a second [PLACE] university; and the program’s archive holds 94 cohort-traceable research outputs that did not exist when the inaugural cohort arrived.

University community should be unable to find a shared asset, process, or resource without a name attached to it. Accountability and review The University Council retains standing oversight of the Stewardship Register, receiving it as a fixed agenda item at each of its ordinary meetings across the plan period. The Executive receives an annual Named Ownership Report, tabling Register coverage, custodian tenure, and escalation performance against the measures in this plan. The [ORGANISATION] monitors the Register’s own review cycle, flagging any steward entry whose due date has passed unattested, and the [ORGANISATION] holds the shared indicators this plan reports against, consistent with the University’s existing evaluation-ecosystem practice. No new committee is created to hold this work; it is carried by the governance structures the University already has, with one addition — every one of those structures will now be able to say, for anything within its remit, who specifically is accountable for it. Each School retains responsibility for naming stewards and custodians within its own remit; the Register’s role is to hold those names in one place and make the absence of one impossible to overlook. Where a School disagrees with a finding of the [ORGANISATION], the matter is escalated to the Executive rather than resolved informally, so that a disputed entry is settled on the record and not simply left blank until someone remembers to revisit it.

The University’s own experience over the current planning period bears this out. Work already published from within our schools has found that a system recolouring a shared kitchenette’s compost-bin lids changed remarkably little about what actually went into them, and that a fault-reporting instrument installed to replace a handwritten log measured its own uptime more confidently than it measured the thing it was installed to track. These are not failures of any single instrument. They are what happens when a great deal of institutional attention goes into measuring and anticipating, and comparatively little goes into the plainer question of who is holding the thing steady in between. This plan sets out to close that gap directly, deliberately, and by name.

Our ambition By 2031, every asset, process, and shared resource the University holds will carry a single named, accountable steward, published on a register anyone in the University community can check. That ambition is deliberately narrower than “improve accountability” and deliberately broader than any one School’s remit. It asks nothing exotic of the University — only that the habit already practised in its most visible instruments, the [ORGANISATION]’s named convenor, the [ORGANISATION]’s named custodians, extend all the way down to the smallest shared thing the University holds. An institution that can name who is —7—

answerable for its research strategy should be equally able to name who is answerable for its noticeboards. We do not expect this ambition to be comfortable. Naming a steward for something previously held in common surfaces, immediately, how little upkeep some things have actually been receiving. That discomfort is not a reason to soften the ambition; it is the ambition working as intended, in year one, before a single new instrument has been built.

A Connected and Accountable Campus Why this matters Committee minutes and process action items too often close without anyone clearly responsible for carrying them forward, and a good decision that dissolves into an unowned action item is functionally indistinguishable from a decision never taken at all. Naming an owner at the point of minuting connects governance to delivery, and connecting the Stewardship Register to the [ORGANISATION] means an asset’s steward and its live status are always read from the same published record. A campus that is well connected on paper — a register here, a dashboard there, a committee structure that maps neatly onto both — is only actually accountable if the same name can be followed from one system to the next without a gap. What we’ll do 1. Require every committee and working-group action item to carry a named owner and a review date at the point it is minuted, with no “for information” placeholder standing in for an owner. 2. Publish an escalation ladder naming who inherits an action when its owner is unavailable, rather than leaving it to whoever next reads the minutes. 3. Integrate the Stewardship Register with the [ORGANISATION] so an asset’s steward and its live status sit on the one published record. 4. Review every standing committee’s terms of reference to confirm it names an owner for each of its recurring outputs, not only for one-off decisions. How we’ll know

• The proportion of action items closed by their originally assigned owner exceeds 90% every year of the plan. • Median time from an escalation trigger to a named successor being confirmed falls to under one week by 2029. • 100% of [ORGANISATION] entries carry a visible, linked steward by the close of the plan period. • Every standing committee’s terms of reference names an owner for each recurring output by the end of 2028.

• Median time between an asset becoming unavailable and its replacement or repair falls by at least half against the pre-Register baseline. • Register update compliance, a steward’s entry reviewed within its due cycle, holds above 95% every year from 2028 onward. • Every newly named steward completes induction within one month of appearing on the Register, with no backlog carried past a single reporting quarter.

Capability Through Clear Custodianship Why this matters Shared research equipment and actively maintained datasets currently rely on inherited knowledge of who looks after what, passed on informally when a custodian moves between labs or leaves the University altogether. Formal, attested custodianship protects research capability directly: an instrument that is calibrated on schedule and handed on cleanly serves every project that depends on it, not just the one that happened to be running when it was last checked. The University’s research strategy already depends, in practice, on this kind of custody working quietly in the background; this priority simply makes that dependency visible, named, and reviewable rather than trusting it to survive the next round of staff turnover by luck.

1. Assign a named custodian to every item of shared research equipment and every actively maintained dataset, published on the research-infrastructure register alongside the Stewardship Register. 2. Require an annual custodianship attestation, renewed or formally reassigned, with a documented succession protocol triggered the moment a custodian departs. 3. Route every custodian-reported fault directly into the relevant lab’s maintenance queue, closing the loop between a report and its resolution. 4. Publish a lightweight custodianship handbook for each equipment category — calibration cadence, fault-reporting steps, succession checklist — so a new custodian inherits a procedure, not just a name. How we’ll know • 100% of shared research equipment carries an active, attested custodian by 2029. • Average custodian tenure at handover exceeds eighteen months, with a documented successor named within a fortnight of any departure. • Equipment fault-to-resolution time falls year-on-year for the remainder of the plan. • Every equipment category carries a published handbook, reviewed at each custodianship handover without exception.

Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters — A grade tells the University what a student achieved; it says very little about whether the student was in the room while achieving it. As teaching moves further across lecture theatres, tutorial rooms, and recorded delivery, the University’s ability to say who actually engaged, and when, has not kept pace with its ability to say who eventually passed. This is not a proposal to make attendance compulsory in spirit — it already is, in every unit outline that lists participation as an expectation. It is a proposal to stop treating that expectation as unenforceable simply because the University has not, until now, looked at the record it was already keeping of whether anyone met it.

What we’ll do — 1. Extend swipe-card readers to every lecture theatre and tutorial room by 2028, matching the coverage already standard in professional and research spaces. 2. Instrument the lecture-capture platform with a recurring engagement ping during recorded and livestreamed delivery, logged against the enrolled student rather than the device. 3. Link swipe-derived and ping-derived attendance to scholarship renewal and progression review, alongside — not instead of — academic performance. 4. Publish a unit-by-unit presence comparison across delivery modes, so a fully online unit and a fully in-person unit are held to the same recorded standard rather than exempted from one another. How we’ll know — —9—

• A published Presence Index for every unit of study will track the gap between enrolment and recorded appearance by 2027. • 100% of first-year units will carry a minimum recorded-attendance threshold before a final grade is released by 2029, with no standing exception carried past a single semester. • By 2031, scholarship and progression panels will receive a presence record alongside every academic transcript they review. • The cross-mode presence comparison will publish for every unit of study by 2030, with no delivery mode carrying a lower recorded-attendance threshold than another.

The Plan applies its own discipline to its own oversight. Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor of the [ORGANISATION], was consulted on the governance design and put the symmetry directly: A plan that asks every part of the institution for a presence record and keeps none of its own is exactly the gap this Plan exists to close, so the Council’s oversight of it will be evidenced by the same join-log data it is asking everyone else to keep. — Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION] Any variance between a published target and the record behind it is reported to Council at the next scheduled meeting, alongside the join-log record confirming who was present to hear it. An annual external review, commissioned by Council and reporting to it alone, checks the presence data behind each published target against the underlying system logs. The review’s findings are published in full alongside the Plan’s own annual presence record, without exception for a finding that reflects poorly on the Plan’s own delivery. Each school and unit nominates a Presence Officer, responsible for reconciling that school or unit’s own record ahead of the quarterly report and for answering, on the record, any variance a supervisor, program convenor, or partnership manager cannot otherwise explain. The role carries no disciplinary function of its own; a Presence Officer holds the record, not the judgement of what any particular gap in it means. That judgement stays with the supervisor, convenor, or manager it has always belonged to — the Officer’s job is only to make sure the record they are judging from is complete before they judge it. The Presence Officer network reports, in turn, to the [ORGANISATION], closing the loop between a single corridor reader and the quarterly figure Council eventually sees.

This is the environment this plan answers. Not a single new pressure, but the accumulation of many small ones, each asking the University to be more certain, earlier, and for longer, about the trajectories it is prepared to back. [ORGANISATION]’s setting sharpens the point rather than softening it. A university that draws its staff, students, and partners from across a single region carries a longer institutional memory of the commitments it has made there than a larger, more transient institution might; a trajectory backed badly is not easily forgotten by the people around it. Place, in that sense, is not a backdrop to this plan but a discipline on it — the University answers, over the decade ahead, to the same community it commits to, and a commitment that does not hold up under evidence will be noticed close to home before it is noticed anywhere else.

Where we are headed By 2031, no commitment [ORGANISATION] makes will outlive the evidence that justified it. This is a narrower ambition than it first sounds, and a more demanding one. It does not mean the University will commit to less, or more slowly. It means that whatever the University commits to — an appointment, an admitted cohort, a partnership, a continuing career — will carry a live account of the trajectory behind it, refreshed on a published schedule rather than assumed to still hold. A university that can show, at any point across the life of a commitment, the evidence that still justifies it, is a university whose confidence in its own decisions can be checked rather than simply taken on faith. That is the institution this plan builds toward. Reaching it means treating evidence of trajectory as infrastructure rather than paperwork: something built once, resourced properly, and maintained on a schedule the University publishes and keeps to, in the same way it maintains any other system its people and partners rely on.

[PLACE] the Trajectory Early Why this matters. [PLACE] the trajectory early moves that discovery to before the offer is drafted, where it is still cheap to be wrong. The appointing panel or admissions committee that reads the trajectory late is not being careless; it is simply working with the only evidence the process gave it, gathered after the decision it was meant to inform. Executive summary This plan commits [ORGANISATION] to a single working principle across the decade ahead: no commitment — to a person, a cohort, or a partner — is made, or continued, without evidence of the trajectory that justifies it. Four strategic pillars carry that principle from the moment an offer is drafted through to the moment a portfolio of evidence is finally retired.

Together, these pillars close a gap the University has lived with for longer than it has been comfortable admitting: that a trajectory, once backed, was rarely checked again. By 2031, evidence of trajectory will accompany every commitment [ORGANISATION] makes and every commitment it renews, reviewed on a cadence the institution publishes and holds itself to.

Other institutions have reached for the same instinct without the same discipline, and the difference shows. A screening step added in response to a single bad outcome, then never revisited, is not evidence practice; it is sediment. Executive summary This Strategic Plan commits [ORGANISATION], across the period 2026-2031, to a single organising idea: that no AI-assisted recommendation affecting a student, staff member, or applicant should take effect without a named person attesting that they have read it and stand behind it. Four strategic priorities carry that commitment from the decision itself through to the capacity to review it, the public’s standing to ask about it, and its survival as the number of such decisions keeps rising.

Together these priorities move the University from a default in which an AI-assisted recommendation is actioned unless someone happens to object, to a default in which it is actioned only once someone specific has attested to it. The initiatives that follow are specific by design: each carries a target, a date, and a mechanism for knowing whether it has been met. Where earlier plans have asked the University to “govern AI responsibly” in the abstract, this plan asks something narrower and considerably harder to fake: that every such decision have exactly one name against it, and that the name mean something. None of the four priorities invents a discipline the University does not already practise somewhere. Each extends a habit already at work in one part of the institution — a named convenor, an attested custodian, a published register — to the specific and fast-growing case of decisions an AI-assisted tool has helped make. That is a deliberate choice: an institution that already knows how to name someone accountable for a research instrument does not need a new capability to do the same for a rostering flag, only the will to apply the existing one without exception, at a volume the existing one was not originally built for. The remainder of this document sets out the operating environment that makes this commitment necessary, the ambition that follows from it, and the four strategic priorities, their initiatives, and their measures in detail, before closing with the phasing, governance, and review arrangements that will carry the plan through to 2031.

Where we stand The sector we work within increasingly expects an institution to be able to account for a specific decision, not simply to gesture at a governance framework that covers decisions in general. [ORGANISATION] welcomes that expectation. It sits close to work this University has pursued for years, across the [ORGANISATION]’ anticipatory-capability agenda and the [ORGANISATION]’s evaluation-ecosystem agenda, and it gives that work a sharper edge to press against. Internally, the number of workflows in which an AI-assisted tool contributes to a decision affecting a person’s standing has grown faster than the University’s capacity to review each one in full. Admissions triage, grant-round shortlisting, shift rostering, procurement exception flags, and a growing list of smaller decisions besides now arrive at a human desk already carrying a recommendation. In most of these workflows, a human is still formally the one who decides. What has grown much less certain, as the volume has risen, is how much of the recommendation that human actually reads before they sign. Other institutions across the sector report the same trajectory, in broadly similar terms: an AI-assisted contribution that began in one or two high-visibility workflows, then spread, workflow by workflow, faster than any single governance framework was drafted to anticipate. Most respond by strengthening the framework. Fewer ask the narrower question this plan starts from — not whether a framework exists, but whether the specific person it names to apply it still has the time to do so. [ORGANISATION] does not regard that gap as a failing unique to us. We do regard it as the gap most worth closing first, precisely because it is the one a framework, on its own, cannot close.

The [ORGANISATION] will extend its watching brief to a wider set of partner networks, and the [ORGANISATION] will carry an explicit retirement clock on every indicator it hosts, so that no score outlives the question it was built to answer without someone having to notice on its behalf. The [ORGANISATION] will introduce a dedicated stream on instrumenting automated decisions, drawing directly on the fare-gate, dashboard, and call-routing work in this report, and Capability Sprint enrolments in Deciding Under Measurement will be met, cohort permitting, with a second offering each year rather than one. None of this will resolve the tension this report keeps returning to: that measuring a system closely enough to trust it usually means building a second system to do the measuring, and that second system will eventually need watching too. The School intends to keep building the instruments anyway, and to keep publishing the ones that told us we were wrong. A community that only measures its successes will, eventually, have nothing left worth measuring.

A five-year partnership with a big-four professional services firm’s retail-advisory practice found a second effect nobody had asked the dashboard to produce: staff increasingly treated an unflagged terminal as a resolved terminal, whether or not anyone had actually looked at it. one stores and five years of shift logs. The dashboard did not get worse at its job over that time. The floor-walk simply stopped keeping pace with it. At one flagship store, the retail-advisory partner’s own staff volunteered to run a parallel floor-walk against the dashboard for six months, checking every unflagged terminal at least once per shift regardless of what the dashboard reported. Dr [PERSON] team read that decline two ways in the report that followed: either the dashboard had genuinely closed the gap, or the floor-walk itself had drifted back into trusting what the dashboard told it. Retiring a trust score An indicator that once told an organisation something useful about whether people trusted an automated decision does not stop being consulted just because it has stopped being accurate. Dr [PERSON] contribution to the [ORGANISATION] over the past five years has been a working protocol for retiring exactly this kind of score — tested, at the invitation of a cooperative research consortium, against four trust indicators the consortium’s member organisations had each kept running for longer than anyone could justify. The protocol does not simply switch an indicator off; it requires whoever inherits the gap to say, in writing, what they will watch instead.

One consortium member had kept a customer-trust score alive for six years after the system it originally measured had been replaced twice over, because the score fed a dashboard three other departments still checked every Monday. Dr [PERSON] team’s retirement protocol forced an uncomfortable meeting: the three departments, asked directly what decision the Monday number actually informed, could not agree on an answer between them. The score was retired within the month. What replaced it, six weeks later, was a shorter, less satisfying number that at least everyone in the room could explain. “An indicator survives contact with a dashboard for as long as someone finds it easier to keep checking than to ask what it is for. The hard part was never building the retirement protocol. It was getting anyone to use it.” — Dr [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

Where we’re headed The next five years will ask a harder question of the School than the last five did. Where this report has mostly measured systems that already made a decision and left a trace behind them, the School’s coming work will lean further into anticipation: catching a handover before it completes rather than auditing it once it has. — 10 —

Catching the handover early Most organisations do not announce the day a decision moves from a person to a system; it simply starts happening more often until nobody remembers the last time a person made the call unassisted. Working with a [PLACE] evaluation agency’s member network, Dr [PERSON] group tested whether giving a workplace explicit advance notice of an approaching automated handover — weeks rather than a single memo — changed how much staff trusted the system six months after it arrived. The [ORGANISATION]’s usual brief is watching when a review is overdue; this

extended the same instinct to watching for a handover before it happened rather than accounting for it afterwards. Across twenty workplace pilots in the agency’s network, sites that received several weeks’ documented notice before an automated system took over a decision reported, on average, higher staff trust in that system at the six-month mark than sites that received a single announcement or none at all — though the relationship was loose enough that several long-notice sites landed no higher than the shortestnotice ones. Dr [PERSON] team resisted the temptation to read the loose relationship as noise: three of the weakest-performing long-notice sites, on closer interview, had given notice of the wrong thing, flagging the tool’s arrival without ever mentioning what decision it would actually make.

Advance notice given before an automated handover, in days, against staff trust in the system at six months, twenty workplace pilots (r = 0.58). Notice alone did not guarantee trust; three of the longest-notice sites clustered among the lowest scores.

“Warning someone a system is coming is not the same as telling them what it will decide. We had to relearn that distinction three times before the notice actually worked.” — Director of Evaluation, a [PLACE] evaluation agency

Director’s reflection Five years ago, a query typed into a University system was still, mostly, a question addressed to a person. That line has not survived intact — not because anyone decided to move it, but because it accumulated, system by system, integration by integration, until a colleague drafting a report, marking an assignment, or triaging a ticket was as likely to be typing to a model as to a form.

This report is the School’s attempt to look at that accumulation directly, with the same instruments it asks everyone else to submit to: a logged count beside an independent audit, printed together rather than reconciled into one figure. The honest answer, five years in, is partial. Some of what the assistants were meant to lighten has genuinely lightened. A good deal of it has simply moved, uncounted, into the work of checking the assistants themselves. We publish both findings, and the gap between them, on the view that a School that measures things for a living owes its own community the same scrutiny it exports everywhere else. Director, [ORGANISATION]

Numbers in context Every system this report examines already keeps a number: a query logged, a ticket auto-triaged, a draft time-stamped, a session closed. None of those numbers, on their own, say anything about workload — only about use. Where this report claims a change in workload, it pairs the system’s own logged count against an independent audit — a time-diary sample, a walked case review, or a matched before/after tasktiming exercise — run by researchers without access to the system’s own dashboard while they worked. The two numbers are reported side by side throughout, not reconciled into one, because reconciling them is the mistake the School is trying to document. A rising —4—

“A tile that only goes up is not, on its own, evidence that anything is going down. We built the audit precisely so the two claims could not be confused for each other.” — Dr [PERSON], Postdoctoral Fellow, [ORGANISATION]

What the assistant actually shortened The [ORGANISATION] exists to trace how research effort becomes counted impact; this period, Dr [PERSON]’s team pointed the same method at a shorter pathway — how a logged assistant interaction becomes a shortened task. The question, stripped of its usual citation-flow framing, was simple: does more logged use predict less time spent. In partnership with a big-four professional services firm running its own AI-copilot efficiency review, the team compared per-consultant query counts against blind timings of matched deliverables completed with and without assistant use. The firm had expected, going in, a roughly linear relationship between queries and delivery speed. The matched timings showed no reliable relationship in either direction once —6—

Evaluating the evaluators, again [ORGANISATION] exists to ask whether a review changes anything beyond recertifying what a panel already believed. Applied to the assistants themselves, its standing method asked a narrower question this period: does adding an AI assistant to a review process shorten the review, deepen it, or simply relocate the same number of hours somewhere else in the cycle.

Working with a [PLACE] evaluation agency piloting an assistant-drafted first pass on its own programme reviews, Dr [PERSON]’s team timed the full review cycle before and after the assistant’s introduction. Draft turnaround fell by nearly half. Total cycle time, from draft to panel sign-off, held within three per cent of the preassistant baseline, the saved drafting hours reabsorbed almost entirely into an additional verification pass the panel had not previously required.

Background Across the registers opened to us, “actioned” was a status conferred by being mentioned. An item raised in 2021 and discussed at forty-one subsequent meetings had, by every register we saw, been actioned forty-one times. The carry count sat in plain view in every minute book — it is what a phrase like carried forward is for — and no collaborator had ever summed it. The number existed; nothing read it.

What we did Working with a services-delivery agency, Lecturer [PERSON]’s team reconstructed the item-level history behind five years of a divisional improvement register: every item, every meeting at which it appeared, and every form of words used to defer it. The reconstruction took eleven months, mostly because deferral has a large vocabulary and the agency’s secretariat had used most of it. From that history the team defined the carry count as a property of the item rather than the meeting,

Outcomes A state museum network ran the instrument across its site committees as the first collaborator to do so unassisted, and its results are the ones we show here because they were the least edited. The network’s open register had not grown much over five years, which its own reporting had read as stability. What the carry count found underneath was ageing: the register was holding roughly the same number of items, and those items were getting steadily older. The museum network’s board had been given a figure about volume when the thing that had changed was duration.

Composition of a museum network’s open register by the number of meetings each item had been carried, across five annual review rounds. Items carried twenty-five or more times were 4% of the open register in 2021 and 42% of it in 2025, with the register’s total size never varying by more than a tenth.

“We had been reporting the size of the list for eleven years. Nobody had ever asked us the age of it, and we did not have a field for the answer.” — Secretariat lead, a state museum network

Review cadence and the open item The [ORGANISATION] asks how often a standing review arrives too late to change anything. This period it turned the question inside out and asked what happens when a review arrives more often than anything can change.

Background A fortnightly action review produces twenty-six opportunities a year to record an item as progressed, and an annual one produces a single opportunity to record it as neglected. Both cadences were common among our collaborators, and both had been chosen on grounds of diligence rather than evidence. Nobody we asked could say what cadence their register was designed for; several could name the meeting the cadence had been inherited from. The Observatory’s own framing had until this period treated cadence as a property of a review body. The registers taught us to treat it as a property of the item: a cadence sets the interval at which an item’s file can be touched, and therefore the resolution at which its history is recorded, but nothing about that interval reaches the work the item is actually waiting on. A committee meeting weekly and a committee meeting yearly are, from the item’s point of view, waiting for the same person to make the same call.

What we did A state audit office asked the Observatory to establish whether its three-weekly improvement cadence was serving its own register. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team paired the office’s carry counts against its closure records for the full period and found that shortening the cadence in 2023 had raised the number of recorded actions per item by about a third while leaving the number of closures per year almost exactly where it had been. The office had bought itself more evidence of attention to the same unfinished work.

Background Not one of the 212 registers opened to us carried a documented way for an item to leave other than being done. Closed and quietly abandoned shared a single field, which meant the field could not be trusted and the register kept everything. Several collaborators told us their oldest items were retained precisely because removing one would require somebody to put their name to the judgement that it had never mattered.

What we did A state audit office trialled a closure protocol drafted with Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team: a lapse route, distinct from completion, requiring a named authoriser, a one-line reason, and publication of the lapsed item on a standing list with no mechanism for removing an entry from it. The protocol was deliberately unkind. An item could be let go, but not silently, and not by a committee as a body.

Outcomes Across eighteen months the office lapsed 340 items, 106 of them older than the register’s retention rule, and reopened 31 — a reopening rate the office regards as the cost of the protocol working and we regard as the most interesting number in this report. A state museum network’s adoption produced a similar pattern at a quarter of the scale. Both collaborators kept the named authoriser and both, when asked, said the naming was the part that changed behaviour; the published list was what made the naming stick. Two [ORGANISATION] were rebuilt around the protocol during this period, and the closure module is now the most-completed unit in the short-course line. The office’s published list of lapsed items has since become a standing agenda paper in its own right, which is either the protocol failing in a new form or the first register this School has encountered that an organisation reads on purpose. “An item nobody will close is an item nobody will own. The protocol did not make those decisions easier. It made them attributable, and that turned out to be sufficient.” — Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON], [ORGANISATION]

Outcomes An engineering peak body then let the Observatory test the inverse, halving the frequency of its national practice committee’s action review for eighteen months. We had expected either an improvement, as items were given room to mature, or a deterioration, as they slipped from view. Neither occurred. The closure rate was statistically indistinguishable from the period before, the carry counts simply accumulated more slowly, and the median item took the same number of months to close while being carried half as often. We report the null result as a null result: on this evidence, cadence governs how much attention an open item is recorded as receiving, and not whether it closes.

“Meeting more often about the same item is not a decision. Our practice committee met twice as often for three years and closed the same number of things, and the honest reading is that we were measuring our own diligence.” — Practice director, an engineering peak body

What counted as finished The [ORGANISATION]’s researchers treat every tile on a self-measurement wall as an object of study rather than a finished product. This period’s fieldwork found one of the plainest tiles yet: a register’s own status field, wired directly to a board that counted every edit as movement.

Background In progress is a status that closes nothing and reads as motion. Where a collaborator’s register fed an ambient board, an item’s carry produced an update, the update produced a timestamp, and the timestamp produced a tile reading green — a chain in which the only step requiring anybody to do anything was the one nobody had to do. The School’s data-cultures theme had seen the shape before in demonstration culture, where a compressed slot decides what counts as finished.

A metropolitan transit authority invited Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team to review the customer-satisfaction tile mounted in its central control room — a single number, refreshed quarterly when the tile first went up, that operations staff had come to check the way they check the time. The team found the figure had not refreshed in over two years; the survey instrument behind it had been discontinued, its contractor reassigned, and nobody in the control room had noticed, because the number on the wall had never stopped looking current. Staff described adjusting rostering and complaint-escalation decisions around a figure that, for the better part of two years, had simply been sitting there. “Nobody lied to us about the number. It just stopped being anyone’s job to keep it honest, and the wall never said so.” — Control Room Supervisor, a metropolitan transit authority

What a number is asked to keep meaning The [ORGANISATION] exists to trace how a piece of research effort becomes counted, valued, and eventually cited work — the usual pathway runs forward, from a finding to its recognition. This period Senior Research Fellow [PERSON]’s team ran the Atlas’s method in reverse on a single class of object: a customer-facing score, taken once for a specific purpose, and asked by everyone downstream to keep meaning the same thing indefinitely.

A national telecommunications carrier had first measured a customer-trust score for a single marketing campaign in 2022, using a bespoke short-form survey run once, to a sample of respondents who saw one advertisement. Four years on, the same figure was still appearing in board papers, investor briefings, and a customer-facing trust page on the carrier’s website — each new citation treating the score as if it had just been taken, none of them noting the year, the sample, or the campaign it was built to evaluate. The Atlas team’s pathway map showed the score picking up eleven distinct downstream citations, only one of which linked back to the original survey instrument.

“A score doesn’t announce its own expiry. Somebody has to keep asking it how old it actually is, and for four years nobody at the carrier had that job.” — Senior Research Fellow [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

Retiring a reading, formally [ORGANISATION] asks what a review actually changes, as distinct from what it merely re-certifies; applied to metric stewardship, this period’s strand of that programme asked a narrower version of the same question — what does it take, procedurally, for an organisation to formally retire a reading it has stopped needing. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team found the honest answer was almost always: more than deciding the number is no longer useful.

A chronic-disease foundation had carried a single wellbeing-index item in its annual report for eleven years, unchanged since the underlying survey instrument it drew from was substituted for a longer, better-validated one in the report’s third year. The item stayed because retiring it required an explicit board resolution nobody had thought to draft, and because the annual report’s template treated the item as a fixed row rather than a chosen one. Working with the School, the foundation drafted its first formal retirement protocol: a standing annual prompt requiring every legacy indicator to be re-justified in writing or struck from the template, with the item in question the protocol’s first formal retirement. “Nobody ever votes to keep a stale indicator. It survives because retiring it was never anybody’s job description, and giving it one turned out to be most of the fix.” — Dr [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

Instruments that outlast their moment The [ORGANISATION] exists to catalogue what an organisation is still measuring and why — not the metrics a partner intends to keep using, but the ones still quietly in circulation years after the review that was meant to retire or renew them. This period the Commons turned its standing method on ratings and scores published once and left running: a compliance figure, a readiness index, a certification level, each still being cited in contract renewals, funding applications, or board papers long after the practice it once measured had moved on. The pattern, once the Commons started counting it, showed up faster than expected — and in places the School had not thought to look first. Working with a state audit office, Senior Lecturer [PERSON]’s team traced a compliance-rating index the office had first published for a routine contractor review in 2021 and never formally revised. The index kept circulating — cited in three subsequent contract renewals, folded into a risk-appetite briefing, referenced once in a ministerial answer — each use treating the figure as current because nothing about its presentation ever suggested otherwise. When the team finally asked the office to re-audit the underlying practice against the original 2021 criteria, the practice had changed twice in the interim; the index, formally, had not. The office’s own review sign-off had lapsed a year before the first of the three renewals that quoted it.

The proxy that stayed on the wall The [ORGANISATION] is the School’s own always-on self-measurement wall, and its researchers treat every tile on it, and every comparable board a partner installs, as an object of study rather than a finished product. A tile is easy to commission and, this period’s fieldwork found, unusually hard to decommission: once a reading earns a fixed position on a wall people walk past daily, its removal starts to read less like housekeeping and more like an admission that something was once being watched and now is not.

It is a printer telling you, at the last possible moment, something it could have told you six pages ago.” — Research Fellow [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION]

The false-empty alert The [ORGANISATION]’s researchers treat every tile on it, and every comparable board a partner installs, as an object of study rather than a finished product. This period’s fieldwork found one of the simplest tiles yet: a fleet’s own “replace cartridge” signal, wired straight into an uptime board with no audit in between. A regional university network’s facilities team had connected its shared printers’ replace-cartridge signal directly to the [ORGANISATION]’s uptime tile, treating every alert as confirmed empty. Lecturer and Convenor [PERSON]’s team logged each alert against an audited toner-mass reading taken within the hour, and found most midweek alerts fired while measurable capacity remained — the tile’s uptime figure was recording a queue of unnecessary cartridge swaps as unplanned downtime.

Recalibration, then drift [ORGANISATION] asks what a review actually changes, as distinct from what it merely re-certifies; applied to a device fleet, this period’s strand of that programme asked the same question of a gauge rather than a policy. Working with a national telecommunications carrier’s back-office print fleet, Postdoctoral Fellow [PERSON]’s team recalibrated five device classes’ gauges against an audited baseline, then returned eighteen months later to re-audit the same devices. Every class had drifted back out of true; the remote-kiosk model drifted furthest, its gauge again reporting comfortably more toner than the audit could find.

What’s next Over the next planning period, the four partnerships in this report become the pilot cohort for a standing quarterly audit cycle rather than a one-off study: each partner’s fleet will carry a re-calibration date, after which a gauge’s continued reporting requires a fresh audit rather than an assumed carry-over. The [ORGANISATION] will offer its early-warning ensemble as a fleet-wide service beyond the one department that piloted it, on the expectation that the lead time it buys stays measured in pages rather than minutes.

The [ORGANISATION] will pilot a rule decoupling an uptime tile from a raw alert count, so that a fleet’s “replace cartridge” signal must clear an audit threshold before it counts as downtime rather than a routine swap. [ORGANISATION] will extend the eighteen-month re-audit into a standing instrument, on the expectation — not yet tested — that a shorter interval between audits produces less drift, rather than merely catching the same drift sooner. None of this promises a gauge that stops being wrong. Measurement, done honestly, tends to find more drift than any fleet gets around to correcting, and the School expects that imbalance to persist well past this reporting period. Its more modest aim is to make the gap between a reading and the thing it reads a little harder to miss.

This KPI assesses the University’s research income collected through the Higher Education Research Data Collection (HERDC) and reflects the University’s performance in securing competitive and collaborative funding. This measure excludes the National Institutes Grant and captures income from competitive grants, other public sector funding, industry/ non-profit income, and Cooperative Research Centre (CRC). Year-on-year trends demonstrate the University’s capacity to attract significant investment for research projects that deliver national and global impact, reinforcing our position as a leading research-intensive university. Reflecting the annual HERDC reporting cycle, research income is verified and reported one year lagged from the current year.

This KPI assesses a five-year average FWCI, excluding the most recent two publication years, which is considered best practice for citation analysis as it allows sufficient time for citations to accumulate and provides a more stable measure of research impact. FWCI is a normalised metric that measures the number of citations received per paper, adjusted for subject area, publication year and document type. A score of 1.0 represents the world average, meaning an FWCI above 1 indicates performance above global norms. Because citation practices vary significantly across disciplines normalisation ensures fair comparison between fields.

This KPI accesses the percentage of HDR candidates who rate their overall experience positively. It is measured through the Postgraduate Research Experience Survey (PRES) on a biennial basis (i.e. 2027, 2029). For the alternate years (i.e. 2026, 2028), it is measured through an [ORGANISATION] internal survey of HDR candidates. PRES is administered from the UK not-for-profit Advance HE, providing benchmarking data for global, [ORGANISATION], and [PLACE] participating universities. Performance is determined using the proportion of respondents who select a positive response to the ‘Overall, I am satisfied with the experience of my research degree program’ question.

The vision of [ORGANISATION] The role of the vision A vision should not only describe a future goal but also be tangible in the present. It should include elements that already exist in some form today and serve as inspiration for our actions. This makes the vision more than just a distant aspiration – it becomes a living guide, ensuring that every step forward is not just movement but real progress and a concrete approach toward its realisation. For this reason, we have chosen a vision that describes how we want to act, think and be in (at most) ten years) - not one that measures success purely by the placements or rankings. We deliberately avoid grand declarations such as "We will be among the best in the world in research area X" or "We will be among the top 50 universities worldwide". This does not mean we doubt our ability to be among the world‘s best. Rather, the danger of such goal-setting lies in narrowing our perspective: a university is not merely a competitor in global rankings but, as universitas, it is also a space for discovery, experimentation and interdisciplinary exchange. Too rigid a definition of success could restrict the very openness that often makes excellent science possible in the first place. Many of the greatest scientific breakthroughs were not planned but the result of serendipity - of fortunate accidents that occur only when researchers have the freedom to pursue new ideas without bias. Relying solely on fixed metrics risks eliminating these opportunities before they can unfold. We cannot predict with certainty which topics, standards or conditions will still be relevant in ten years. What seems ambitious today may soon become outdated or taken for granted – or turn out to be a dead end. Likewise, what is considered a niche scientific topic today may be thrust into the spotlight tomorrow.

Media from a historical and cultural perspective One of the genuine tasks of the Faculty is to study media as means of transmission, of communication, and mediation of expressions and phenomena of cultural history. The types and origins of sources are indeed diverse – some of them (still) remain in the landscape or under the soil, others are preserved in the Faculty’s collections or in museums, in archives and libraries, or they are generated by means of interview research or participant observation. The

valorisation and interpretation of these sources requires special theories and methods that need to be determined in an interdisciplinary dialogue. Media history and media criticism constitute an essential basis for any research in the fields of cultural studies and/or history. These phenomena of cultural history can, and must, be integrated into the discourse on history. They convey diverse meaning and, when viewed against the background of history, can be understood in their complexity. In the present day, the cultural history of communication, illustrated also through its material evidence, is a subject of immediate relevance. This thematic area is explored particularly within the key research areas of material culture; and visual cultural history: cultures and media of the visual; and also in the area of text and edition – editorial studies. In this respect, the key research areas of history of visual culture: cultures and media of the visual, with a historical focus, and the area of visual studies in the social sciences at the Faculty of Social Sciences, with the focus on photography and film, complement each other.

Biomolecules for a healthy lifespan Our disability-free life expectancy is considerably shorter than general life expectancy. So far, measures aiming to increase the lifespan spent in good health have mostly been limited to adapting one’s lifestyle. The effects of biomolecules of the primary and secondary metabolisms – which are either endogenously produced by the organism itself, or exogenously originating – on health and age-related physiological changes have not yet been studied to a sufficient degree. The goals of the key research area of biomolecules for a healthy lifespan are thus oriented towards (i) understanding the modes of action of biomolecules and natural products of pharmaceutical relevance in health-related biological processes at the molecular, cellular and organismal levels, (ii) examining their influence on the number of years spent in good health, and (iii) identifying new biologically active natural products and their targets. The results will help to characterise biomolecules which have a positive effect on life expectancy and possibly on the number of years in good health. Additionally, this research will help to discover the mechanisms by which these biomolecules act. This topic is being discussed as a central research area within the new [ORGANISATION] programme.

The goals in this key research area include strengthening the cognitive and behavioural sciences as well as neuroscience, and intensifying the academic interactions between neuroscience, cognition, pharmacy and the nutritional sciences. The activities in the context of this key research area contribute to enhancing inter-faculty collaboration and to establishing cooperation with relevant research groups in and around [PLACE] (IMP Research Institute of Molecular Pathology, IMBA Institute of Molecular Biotechnology and IST Institute of Science and Technology [PLACE]).

Outlook In the current government programme for the period 2020–2024, the Federal Government is committed to “ensuring the best possible funding and planning security [...] for [PLACE] universities”20. This needs to be done in any case for the next two performance agreement periods: “Universities will receive funding commitments with indexations for the next performance agreement periods until 2027.”21 Furthermore, the government programme provides for the “consistent continuation and further development of the ‘new university funding scheme’ with all initiated implementation steps”22. The ‘new university funding scheme’ has enabled a growth path for teaching and research capacities since 2019. Student-teacher ratios can now be improved and research priorities can be set. Compared to the University of [PLACE], but also to universities of excellence in [PLACE], the [ORGANISATION] still has a lot of catching up to do in terms of student-teacher ratios and research capacities, but also in terms of access to sufficient research (funding) resources. In a national comparison, the [ORGANISATION], despite its growth path in the period 2019–2021, is the university whose student-teacher ratios remain significantly below the average of comparable universities. For the [ORGANISATION], it is therefore crucial that the stipulations of the government programme can be adhered to and are backed by sufficient financial resources and that the specific situation of the [ORGANISATION] with regard to the student-teacher ratios is taken into account in the distribution of funds. In addition to sustainable funding for universities, strengthening the financial resources for basic research is a high priority for the [ORGANISATION]. In particular, the funding of the [PLACE] Science Fund (FWF) must be brought up to the level of comparable [PLACE] research funding organisations in order to ensure access to sufficient competitively awarded funds in view of the increase in the number of professorships and tenure track positions.

2.2.2 Lifelong learning, executive education: certificate programs and other continuing education offerings Lifelong learning (LLL) is the concept of continuous learning throughout a person’s life. It includes the aim of providing greater educational opportunities to disadvantaged groups and eliminating inequalities in the long term (GUEP implementation objectives 3c and 4c). When it comes to lifelong learning, WU follows the definition proposed by the [PLACE] Commission, which defines lifelong learning as “all learning activity undertaken throughout life, with the aim of improving knowledge, skills and competences within a personal, civic, social and/or employment-related perspective.”8 Certain third mission activities, such as the Market Day or the Children’s University, are designed to give primary school students, especially those from at-risk schools, a taste of the university experience. WU’s recruiting is also aimed specifically at young people whose parents do not have a university degree (“first-generation students”) and who come from educationally disadvantaged backgrounds. One way in which WU does this is through partnerships and collaborations with secondary schools (GUEP implementation objective 3a). As a responsible university, WU aspires to be an important institution for lifelong learning in [PLACE] and strives to live up to this commitment with its regular degree programs and the continuing education offerings at the WU Executive Academy. WU’s efforts in this regard are a way of meeting its responsibility to society, as economic and institutional knowledge is directly linked to a proper understanding of democracy and a greater acceptance of evidence-based knowledge (see GUEP, p. 10). In developing its LLL strategy and setting its priorities, WU orients itself to the “student life cycle”9 (GUEP implementation objective 3a). It strives to develop and offer educational formats that are appropriate for the target group in order to contribute to the economic competitiveness of individuals and of [PLACE] as a business location (GUEP system objective 5). Organised through the WU Executive Academy, the university offers continuing education for working professionals (with or without prior university education). For example, WU’s Plan for the Advancement of Women, Equal Opportunities Plan, and Guidelines for the Inclusion of Employees with Disabilities illustrate this commitment. WU strives to live up to these responsibilities on all levels, particularly when it comes to management positions. To WU, diversity encompasses social categories as much as features related to the individual and the organisation. WU does not stop at safeguarding against discrimination based on age, disability, ethnicity, gender, religion or ideology, or sexual orientation as stipulated by law, but above and beyond that, it also strives to overcome stereotypes related to these dimensions. This is why WU’s programs for the advancement of diversity and inclusion are focusing increasingly on biographical contexts and the disadvantages associated with them. This approach has already been applied in assessing the performance of professors as well as in programs intended to help employees reconcile private and family life more easily with their professional responsibilities. With these activities, WU acknowledges that balancing family life and work is a major challenge for many people in its workforce. WU is committed to its role as a responsible employer and is working continuously to create a university that allows its employees to successfully balance work and private life (GUEP implementation goal 4a). This is why WU has been part of the “hochschuleundfamilie” auditing program since 2013. This program supports universities in implementing measures to help employees balance work and private life and also helps identify potential for improvement within the organisation.
